data.title: Commerce that belongs in EmDash.
data.description: Open-source commerce tools for your EmDash site, with hosted services being built to make setup simpler.

layout.heading: An EmDash foundation
layout.body: Keep your storefront and content in EmDash. DinkusKit is building the catalog, checkout, inventory and payments connections around it.

layout.heading: Inventory, coming soon
layout.body: Hosted Inventory is coming soon and is not required to start with Commerce. You will keep stock in EmDash when that service is ready. An open-source self-host path will be documented; neither path is provisioned on this website today.

layout.heading: Your Stripe account
layout.body: The planned Payments plugin connects your own Stripe account through hosted setup. Customers pay your business through Stripe.

layout.heading: Follow the build
layout.body: You can create a local DinkusKit account on this website. Hosted inventory and payments activation are still being prepared. Explore the source on GitHub and read Getting started for the intended installation experience.

data.title: Your site. One connected experience.
data.description: The first DinkusKit experience is for people who already have an EmDash site.

layout.heading: 1. Create an EmDash site
layout.body: Follow the official EmDash installation guide to scaffold a site with npm create emdash@latest. Official themes are complete Astro templates. This website is not an installer.

layout.heading: 2. Connect your DinkusKit account
layout.body: Sign in with your DinkusKit account. Authorizing a site still requires verified site control from Inventory Connect; this website will not accept a typed site ID. The same account will be able to connect multiple stores once that protocol exists. Hosted onboarding and documented open-source self-hosting are not provisioned here.

layout.heading: 3. Commerce and Template Store
layout.body: Commerce and the Template Store will be released together as a verified pair. You can try the interactive storefront in the playground: each visitor gets their own throwaway store with a synthetic catalog to test browsing and cart behavior. Checkout shows as unavailable, so no real purchases can be made. Template Store setup guidance is available for the development source pilot, while released installable packages and artifacts remain pending.

layout.heading: Trial access
layout.body: Initial hosted Inventory access is planned as a trial without payment details and is not a prerequisite for Commerce. Trial duration, usage limits and pricing have not been set.

data.title: You've tried the playground. Now run your own.
data.description: Your store is an EmDash site you own. DinkusKit adds the shop: Commerce for products and orders, Payments for card checkout, and Ship for postage. Four steps get you from nothing to a test order.

layout.heading: Three plugins make the shop
layout.body: Each one installs from the plugin Registry in your EmDash admin.

layout.signed_out_text: Your store connects to a DinkusKit account.

layout.heading: Your four steps
layout.done_message: That's a working store in test mode. Live payments open after DinkusKit's own real-store proof.

layout.heading: Have an EmDash site
layout.body: DinkusKit runs inside your own EmDash site, so you keep your site, your content and your customers.
layout.more_body: Follow the EmDash install guide. It creates a site you can run on Cloudflare in a few minutes. Pick any theme; you can change it later.

layout.heading: Add Commerce, Payments and Ship
layout.body: In your store admin, open the plugin Registry and install DinkusKit Commerce, DinkusKit Payments and DinkusKit Ship. Ship is optional if you'd rather mark orders shipped by hand.

layout.heading: Press Connect to DinkusKit
layout.body: Connect Commerce first; it registers your store with your DinkusKit account. Then press Connect in Payments and in Ship. Each press asks you to sign in here, and the business owner approves the store once.
layout.note: The Connect button arrives with the next Commerce, Payments and Ship releases.

layout.heading: Add a product and place a test order
layout.body: Add a product with a price, open your shop, and check out with the test card 4242 4242 4242 4242, any future date and any three digits. The order shows up in Commerce, ready to ship.

layout.heading: Want to look around first?
layout.body: Go back to the playground, or read how DinkusKit fits together.

When the change belongs in core

Commerce owns authoritative price, checkout attempts, inventory-provider binding, and the provider ports. Payments owns isolated processor adapters and server-side processor selection. Extending those contracts may require coordinated versioning, tests, and review in the owning repository.
Do not create a second order writer, override a failed provider with local state, or infer a supported new processor from a TypeScript interface. Follow

data.title: Make and verify a core contribution
data.summary: Choose the owning repository, make one focused change, and report the evidence for review.
data.version_scope: Commerce e8eca124 and Payments b92ec308 source instructions

children.text: Keep the change with the module that owns the behavior. The website repository owns this documentation and site presentation. Commerce owns catalog, authoritative pricing, checkout orchestration, and orders. Payments owns provider transport and connection status. Inventory and Ship own their respective product boundaries.

, charter, contribution guide, and verification scripts before editing. The commands below were reconciled against the pinned Commerce and Payments sources; they are not a universal command set for every DinkusKit repository.

on a dedicated branch. Keep one product or infrastructure slice per pull request, preserve unrelated work, and identify the expected behavior before changing it. The inspected repositories require product decisions to pass through their GrillTrack workflow before implementation.
. After selecting that runtime, their agent instructions call for:

The agent-skills command installs each repository's pinned tooling. Read and maintain the decision ledger through its CLI; do not hand-edit it. These setup commands have not been run as a full contributor environment proof for this draft.

Commerce's quick wrapper includes typechecking, unit tests, and repository audits. Full adds integration, sandbox, native-consumer, and settings checks. Payments' quick wrapper includes tests, typechecking, and its repository audit. Full adds Worker/runtime checks, builds, plugin validation, build-identity checks, and plugin-runtime tests. Read the matching verification skill for local prerequisites and browser/runtime requirements.

Add tests for observable changed behavior, including failures that must remain unavailable rather than succeeding through fallback. For a Registry product, verify the Registry build; a native-only result is not sufficient evidence of the supported merchant path.

Payments requires each pull request to declare a version bump with Changesets or an explicit empty changeset for non-bumping work. Its documented beta-to-stable flow is separate from ordinary contribution checks. Consult the owning repository's current release instructions instead of publishing a package as part of a routine contribution.

Explain the problem, the change, and the resulting behavior. Report the exact commit and environment checked, the commands that passed, any required checks that could not run, and the limits of fixture or synthetic-provider evidence. Link public-safe evidence for the changed behavior.

Keep credentials, customer data, payment details, and private operational material out of source, logs, screenshots, and pull-request text. Do not import unrelated repository history or private proof bundles. These repositories treat every committed byte as immediately public.

Merging, package publication, deployment, production mutation, and live payment traffic are distinct actions with their own approval gates. A passing test suite or automated review does not authorize them.

data.version_scope: Source review at 2b51314c7150; private 0.0.0 packages; no installable release verified

children.text: Inventory owns physical stock: SKU identities, locations, quantities, reservations, movements, and receipts.
owns products, prices, checkout, and orders. A storefront must use those authorities instead of maintaining another stock counter.

This reference describes the reviewed source and its product contracts. It does not establish an available Registry installation or a supported production setup. For the initial store journey, begin with

The product contract distinguishes unmanaged and managed products. An unmanaged product uses Commerce's manual availability and sends no stock commands. A managed product uses exactly one configured inventory provider. DinkusKit Inventory is the default and only first-party provider in the v1 contract; a conforming third-party provider is an advanced integration boundary, not an established installable add-on SDK.

The current Template Store shipping profile keeps Inventory off. Its managed-stock demonstration is a separate development profile. This is why Inventory must not be listed as a universal prerequisite for the first test order. Older descriptions of Commerce and Inventory launching together describe product direction; they do not prove a mandatory dependency or a released managed-stock configuration.

Existing managed products must retain their identity and configuration. If their provider is missing, incompatible, or unavailable, the contract refuses stock-dependent operations. It does not convert the product to unmanaged or substitute a local quantity.

An inventory pool groups stock under one authoritative ledger. Each physical location has its own quantities, and each storefront connection has an explicit fulfillment location. Matching product names or SKUs do not establish that mapping.

content.text: Physical stock currently recorded at the location.
Stock committed to leave the location.
On hand minus reserved stock and outgoing commitments.
Stock committed to arrive but not yet dispatched.
Dispatched stock that has not yet been received.

children.text: For example, ten on hand with three reserved and two committed to a transfer leaves five available. Expected and in-transit stock do not increase current availability.

The command contract requires a stock change and its immutable receipt to commit together. Opening stock begins with a physical count and reviewed opening balances. Later corrections create new movements; they do not rewrite old receipts.

A successful preview changes no stock. A confirmation must return a committed result before the caller treats the change as complete. After a timeout, the outcome is unknown: resolve or retry the original command identity with the same contents. Creating a replacement command could apply the change twice.

The reviewed source includes SKU registration, initial-stock and adjustment previews and confirmations, stock views, and location-move controls in the EmDash plugin. It also contains hosted routes and reservation/transfer kernels. This establishes implementation scope in source, not proof that every operation is available to a particular installed store.

The service's provider implementation supports the Pitney Bowes sandbox. Live postage is not implemented in the inspected source. A sandbox PDF and tracking number are not postage for mailing a parcel.

children.text: A TEST order remains TEST through either path. The code refuses to buy postage for a TEST order outside the sandbox. For non-TEST orders, the implemented account path requires the owner's connected postage account, but its current provider connection is still sandbox-only.

Commerce sends an authenticated, versioned order record. Ship accepts the current or a newer order version and does not overwrite it with an older delivery. The admitted shipping record includes a US destination and line quantities. Billing details and payment credentials are outside that record.

The owner-page source provides package weight and service review, prices, label creation, PDF printing, and cancellation. A label purchase requires a deliberate owner action. Ship stores the label PDF and queues tracking for Commerce to collect and acknowledge. These are source contracts, not a claim that the same flow has been tested on your site.

If a provider response is lost, the source attempts to reconcile the original transaction before allowing a new purchase. Cancellation concerns the label; it does not cancel or refund the Commerce order. Payment refunds belong to the payment/order workflow.

children.text: Separate plugin installation, store connection, processor configuration, storefront rendering, and order persistence. They use different contracts, so a successful step does not prove the next one. Record the exact message, affected stage, and versions before changing settings.

data.title: Read the docs from your coding assistant
data.summary: Use the same version-scoped articles as the website and keep documentation access separate from store administration.
data.version_scope: Draft publishing foundation; public docs MCP and client verification pending

children.text: The documentation is authored as Markdown in the website repository. The HTML page, native Markdown endpoint, human search data, and discovery file are intended to come from the same selected articles. An assistant should read that source rather than relying on a separate, manually maintained agent guide.

Each article includes product and version scope. Ask your assistant to compare that scope with the repository or installed artifact it is changing. A source-backed example is not proof that another version exports the same contract.
This contribution contains article drafts. Local development can preview them, but drafts are excluded from production HTML and Markdown, the public search index, and

. Local development also exposes draft Markdown through the article’s Copy as Markdown and View as Markdown actions. A missing article or an empty public index must not be worked around by requesting arbitrary repository files through a documentation API.
The implemented route design for selected, published articles is:

These are implementation routes, not a claim that they are already live on dinkuskit.com. In production, while every article remains a draft, Markdown requests return not found, public search returns an empty array, and
returns not found. Approved publication and deployed-route checks must precede connection instructions aimed at the live site.
A useful request is: “Find the article for integrating the installed public catalog. Read its version scope and sources, compare them with my project, and explain the mismatch before proposing code.”

Have the assistant follow links to the canonical reference instead of duplicating an API description from memory. For a test checkout, require both provider-confirmed TEST payment and the corresponding Commerce Orders record. Never let a browser return or a generated example become evidence that a payment succeeded.

The planned MCP is a small read-only search-and-fetch service over the selected public articles. It is not implemented or client-qualified in this contribution. There is no connection command to copy yet.

Before this section becomes a connection tutorial, verify an actual client, transport, endpoint, search query, and article fetch. Results must include titles, canonical source URLs, and version context. Unknown or private article IDs must return no content. Retrieval must not accept arbitrary paths or fetch arbitrary URLs.

The public docs MCP must expose no CMS, merchant, payment, or mutation tools, and must require no administrative token. Giving an assistant documentation access does not authorize it to modify a store.
. Exact client instructions and a tested search-and-fetch transcript remain a publication gate for this article.
